answer.exemplar: Leverage in bargaining comes from dependence, and only the union can withhold something the ministry needs, namely the loss of production from a stoppage, so it can credibly make the wage rule more expensive to refuse. The association's members can be individually replaced and its services will be bought from someone else, so refusing costs the ministry little and the association has no fallback. The predictable result is that terms move toward the union, not because it argued better but because its non-agreement has a real cost, and the same reasoning explains why professional bodies usually win detail and representation rather than pay.

answer.exemplar: The statute delivered the specific thing members had organised to achieve, so the reason to stay has gone and the more expensive work of enforcement begins. Inspections still have to be funded, staff trained, sanctions applied to owners who ignore the findings, and courts and agencies made to cooperate, and that work needs officials and parties who hold office rather than a protesting membership. A movement that has won its demand therefore has to be rebuilt as a watchdog or a party, because a statute on its own delivers nothing to anyone who is not left holding it in place.

questions.explanation: This item tests the difference between achieving a movement's stated goal and sustaining the conditions that make the goal count. Members leave because the grievance that recruited them has been answered, not because the cause has been abandoned, and the remaining work of inspection, funding and prosecution is routine administration carried by parties and officials. A movement has to be reconstituted as an enforcing body, which is a different organisation from a mobilising one.

answer.exemplar: The two changes act on different things. Internet voting on any device lowers the cost of reaching a ballot box for people without transport, long hours or a fixed address, so it can widen participation; it also makes the count harder to observe independently, which is a loss for scrutiny, not a gain for participation. Lifting spending limits adds more political speech and more agenda competition, which broadens influence for organised groups but lets money dominate attention for everyone else. What the measures produce is a faster, more measurable contest, so measured turnout may rise while the number of citizens who can influence anything has not.

questions.explanation: This item separates the price of taking part from the ease of observing who took part, and from the distribution of influence afterwards. Removing access barriers can widen participation, easing the count improves measurement rather than access, and removing spending limits increases the volume of political communication that money can buy. A rising turnout figure therefore settles nothing on its own, which is why the answer must address each change separately.
questions.hint: Separate who can now take part from how easily the result is observed.

The reversed-opinion answer asserts the opposite without measuring it, and the demands answer converts a sampling problem into a judgement about policy content, which is a different failure entirely.
